Step 9 of 17
A statechart changes the drawing, not the behavior
Send one event to both representations.

The same events run through both representations. The guided run sends PLAY, MUTE, then PAUSE; both end paused and muted. Use the buttons to continue the comparison. A statechart can be flattened into an ordinary state machine by naming each active combination; it packages the rules more compactly.

Step 17 of 17
Use the two signs, then test the boundary
Try POWER_OFF, then POWER_ON. What returns?

Return to the frother inside on: the machine is grinding while the frother is frothing. Press POWER_OFF, then POWER_ON. Both regions exit, then their start dots choose idle and still; no history remembers frothing. Use a parent for a shared transition. Use regions for independent choices. Flattening preserves the behavior, but repeats those rules.

One state at a time.

A coffee machine is a state machine: it is idle, grinding, brewing or ready. An event follows an arrow to the next state.

Try START → GROUND → BREWED → TAKE. An event with no arrow does nothing.

04 / 15 01 / A parent state
Give the box the arrow.

Put the four working states inside on. A POWER_OFF arrow from on applies to any active child. One arrow replaces four copies.

A parent is active when its child is active. Events try the inner state first, then its parent. Here no child handles POWER_OFF.
